848.title: Manresa
848.hook: Ignatius spends months in a cave praying and writes notes that become the Spiritual Exercises
848.howItsDone: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises on retreats, either as a silent retreat away from home or in daily life over a longer stretch, with a guide who meets them regularly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pamplona: a cannonball, a sickbed, and nothing to read but saints. Your line was the cannonball. Today the soldier gets up and walks.

A notebook, in the hand of a man dressed in sackcloth. On his way here he had stopped at the shrine of Our Lady at Montserrat, hung up his sword and dagger, and given his fine clothes to a beggar. He meant to stay a few days in the small town down the hill. He stayed far longer, begging for food, letting his hair and nails grow, praying for hours every day. Tradition points to a cave above the river where he went to pray. And all the while he kept writing in that notebook. The town is Manresa.
screen: `A SWORD LEFT AT MONTSERRAT.` → `A FEW DAYS BECOME A LONG STAY.` → `A NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: Manresa was no peaceful retreat; his own account shows four sides of it. First, the dark. He was tormented by scruples, the fear that he hadn't confessed his sins fully. He confessed again and again and found no rest. He says he was tempted to despair, and he doesn't hide it. Second, the school. Later he described how God dealt with him there the way a schoolmaster deals with a child, one lesson at a time. He wasn't learning from books, but from what happened in him when he prayed. Third, the river. One day, sitting by the river Cardoner, he says the eyes of his understanding began to open. He saw no vision, he says, but understood many things about faith and learning, and everything seemed new. Fourth, the notes. Through it all, he wrote down what he noticed: what helped, what pulled him under, which way of praying led where. Reworked over years, those notes became a small handbook called the Spiritual Exercises. It isn't a book to read straight through. It's a set of instructions for someone guiding another person through prayer, step by step. Some readers hear an echo of Mary in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Ignatius kept them on paper. A soldier who knew nothing about prayer paid close attention, and wrote it down.

segments.voice: If you pray, pray a little while in whatever way you usually do; if you don't, just sit and let your mind be still. Then ask one plain question: what did I notice? A word that stayed, a feeling that came or went, a person who came to mind; don't judge it, and if you like, put it into one line on paper.

849.title: The Society of Jesus (1540)
849.hook: seven friends at Paris become an order, for the greater glory of God
849.howItsDone: Jesuits and students in Jesuit schools often write AMDG, for Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, at the top of their work, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering of everything they'll do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Manresa: scruples, a river, and a notebook that became the Spiritual Exercises. Your line was notes from a cave. Today the notebook finds friends.

Ignatius is back in school. In Paris he sits in class, older than the students around him, starting again from the basics. He has decided that to help people, he needs to study. At the university he shares rooms with two younger men, Pierre Favre and Francis Xavier. One by one, a small band of friends gathers around him. On a hill above Paris, at Montmartre, they make vows together. They don't yet know they're founding anything. The world will end up calling them Jesuits.
screen: `A GROWN MAN LEARNING GRAMMAR.` → `ROOMMATES IN PARIS.` → `VOWS AT MONTMARTRE.`

segments.voice: First, the plan that failed. The friends meant to go to Jerusalem and live where Jesus lived. They waited in Venice for a ship, and no pilgrim ship sailed. So they turned to their backup plan: go to Rome and offer themselves to the pope, to be sent wherever he thought best. A failed plan set the shape of everything after. Second, the name. When people asked who they were, they answered: the Company of Jesus, since they had no head but him. In Latin, the Society of Jesus. Pope Paul the Third approved them as a religious order, and Jesuit is the everyday name that stuck. Third, the motto: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God. Not glory. Greater glory. The question is always comparative: of the choices in front of me, which serves God more? It echoes Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Fourth, the habit of mind. These weren't monks behind walls. They went where they were sent: schools, ports, courts, slums, mission lands. Ignatius asked them to find God in all things, not only in chapel. Over the centuries the Jesuits have been praised, feared, opposed, even suppressed for a time and then restored, with admirers and critics inside the Church and out. The motto hasn't changed. Some Catholic students still write the letters A, M, D, G at the top of their schoolwork.
screen: `THE PLAN THAT FAILED: NO SHIP.` · `THE COMPANY OF JESUS.` · `GREATER GLORY, NOT JUST GLORY.` · `FIND GOD IN ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `AD MAIOREM DEI GLORIAM.`

segments.voice: Picture the rest of your day all at once: the work, the conversations, the errands, the boring parts. If you pray, offer the whole day to God, in your own words or with Paul's: whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God. If you don't, choose one thing ahead of you and decide to do it as well as you can, for something bigger than you.

850.title: Francis Xavier (1506–1552)
850.hook: he baptizes across India and Japan and dies off the coast of China
850.howItsDone: Catholics keep Francis Xavier's feast, and he is honored as a patron of missions; his remains are venerated in Goa, India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesuits: a failed pilgrimage, an offer to the pope, and a motto. Your line was for the greater glory. Today one of Ignatius's roommates is sent east.

The ending comes first. A small island off the coast of China, a hut, a fever, and a man waiting for a boat that never comes. He plans to slip into the mainland, where foreigners are forbidden, and he's been told it could cost him his freedom or his life. He's still waiting when he dies. Behind him lie India, the islands of the spice trade, and Japan. He was once a promising young teacher in Paris, rooming with an older student who kept asking him an uncomfortable question. The older student was Ignatius. The young teacher was Francis Xavier.
screen: `AN ISLAND OFF CHINA.` → `A BOAT THAT NEVER COMES.` → `ONCE A TEACHER IN PARIS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Ignatius kept repeating one line of the Gospel to his ambitious roommate, from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" Xavier wanted a career. That question slowly turned him around. Then, the sending. When the king of Portugal asked for missionaries for India, another Jesuit was chosen and fell ill. Xavier was sent instead, almost overnight. He never saw Ignatius again. Then, the road. In India he walked the coast, taught children prayers in their own language, and baptized. He went on to the islands, and to Japan, where he learned that his ragged clothes made people take him less seriously, not more, and changed his approach. Then China, whose mainland he never reached. All along, Xavier wrote long letters home to his brothers in Europe, and they were copied and read aloud. In one he wishes he could run through the universities of Europe shouting to the students about the people waiting for someone to come. It's also true that his travels went by Portuguese ships, inside a trading empire, and that empire's record is a hard one. The Church names him a patron of the missions. His line, if he had one, was always further.
screen: `WHAT DOTH IT PROFIT A MAN?` · `SENT IN ANOTHER MAN'S PLACE.` · `INDIA, THE ISLANDS, JAPAN.` · `LETTERS READ ALOUD IN EUROPE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS FURTHER.`

851.title: Teresa on the road
851.hook: Teresa founds seventeen convents traveling in rough carts
851.carry: a bad night in a bad inn
851.howItsDone: Discalced Carmelite nuns and friars still live by the reform Teresa began, and Catholics read her Foundations, her Life and the Interior Castle as spiritual classics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis Xavier, from a Paris classroom to an island off China. Your line was always further. Today, another traveler, on rougher roads closer to home.

The roads of Castile are dirt, and a covered cart lurches along one of them. Inside, a few nuns sit in the heat and the dust, with the curtains drawn. At night they stop at an inn, where the beds are bad, the food is worse, and the other guests are loud. In the morning they climb back in. The nun in charge is often sick, and writing a book about the journey as she goes. Her name is Teresa of Avila.
screen: `A CART IN THE DUST.` → `A BAD INN, A LOUD NIGHT.` → `A SICK NUN WRITING IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Teresa is known for prayer: the interior castle, the soul as a garden. But she also spent years on the road, founding new convents of her reformed Carmelites, and she wrote it all down in a book called the Foundations. First, the roads. She describes heat, floods, rivers to cross, and getting lost. She doesn't make it sound holy. She makes it sound tiring. Second, the houses. At one town, she says, the little group arrived in the middle of the night, set up an altar, and had Mass at dawn. Only in daylight did she see how much the walls were crumbling. She was dismayed, and stayed. Third, the inn. In her Way of Perfection, Teresa compares this life, seen from heaven, to one bad night in a bad inn. It's a joke, and it isn't. Uncomfortable, yes, but it's one night, and morning comes. Some readers hear the same idea in the Letter to the Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we have not here a lasting city, but we seek one that is to come." Fourth, the humor. Teresa is funny on the page. She grumbles, laughs at herself, and admits when she's scared. People still tell of her falling from a cart into a river and complaining to God about how he treats his friends. That one comes from stories told about her, not from her own books, but it sounds like her. Holiness, in her hands, was not a calm road. It was a cart that kept moving.

segments.voice: Name one hard stretch you're on right now, a job, a recovery, a relationship, a long wait, and picture it as a road, with you in the cart. Don't pretend it's comfortable; just ask what the next mile is, only the next one. If you pray, hand the road to God the way Teresa did, complaints and all; if you don't, simply breathe with it, and let the morning be coming.

852.title: Philip Neri (1515–1595)
852.hook: the laughing saint of Rome, who taught with jokes and music
852.howItsDone: Oratorian communities in cities around the world still hold gatherings of prayer, talk and music in Philip Neri's style, and the priests live together without vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa in her cart, laughing at herself on rough roads. Your line was a bad night in a bad inn. Today, a saint remembered for his laughter.
screen: `A BAD NIGHT IN A BAD INN.`

segments.voice: An upstairs room in Rome, crowded in the afternoon. Young men from the shops and the banks, a few priests, some students, sitting on benches. Someone reads a page from a saint's life. A priest in a worn cassock asks what they made of it, and the talk goes around the room. Then someone sings. More talk, and somebody laughs. Nobody here is a monk. Nobody took a vow to come. The priest is Philip Neri, and the room gave its name to today's word: Oratory.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN ROME.` → `A READING, A QUESTION, A SONG.` → `NOBODY TOOK A VOW.`

segments.voice: Philip came to Rome from Florence as a young layman and spent years praying in churches and, tradition says, in the catacombs by night, and talking with anyone in the streets. He became a priest later, and he never stopped talking with people. Then, the room. An oratory is a place of prayer, smaller than a church. Philip's gatherings grew so large they needed one, and the group that ran them became the Congregation of the Oratory: priests living together without vows, held only by charity. Then, the music. Philip wanted the meetings to be something people looked forward to. Musicians sang hymns and spiritual songs in the language of the street, so a shopkeeper could follow along. And the jokes. Tradition remembers Philip as the laughing saint. Stories say he shaved half his beard, or read silly books in front of important visitors, so nobody would take him for holy. In one, a woman confesses to gossip. He tells her to pluck a chicken while walking through the streets, then go back and gather every feather. She can't, of course. That, he says, is what gossip is like. Whether every story happened or not, the laughter was the point: it kept him humble and kept sadness from settling in. Some readers hear his spirit in a line from Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." For Philip, joy was not a reward for being holy. It was part of the road.
screen: `A LAYMAN IN THE STREETS OF ROME.` · `A ROOM BECOMES AN ORATORY.` · `SONGS IN THE STREET'S LANGUAGE.` · `HALF A BEARD, AND THE FEATHERS.` · then, large: `REJOICE IN THE LORD ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Smile a little, even if it feels silly, and think of someone who could use a lighter day. What makes them laugh: a memory you share, a ridiculous photo, a joke that's on you, not on anyone else? If you pray, thank God for laughter, and for them; if you don't, simply enjoy picturing their face when it lands.

853.title: Charles Borromeo (1538–1584)
853.hook: a rich reforming bishop who stayed in Milan through the plague
853.howItsDone: Catholics honor Charles Borromeo as a patron of bishops, seminarians and catechists, and seminaries named for him still train priests.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip Neri, half a beard and a room full of songs. Your line was holy joy. Today, a very different saint: serious, thin, and stubborn about one thing.

Plague in Milan. Shops shut, streets empty, carts collecting the dead. Those who can afford to leave the city are leaving, and some of the officials go with them. One carriage is going the other way. The archbishop, who had been away, comes back in. He's from a wealthy, powerful family, and the nephew of a pope. He could have stayed safely away. Instead he walks the streets, visits the sick, and organizes food and care. His name is Charles Borromeo.
screen: `PLAGUE IN MILAN.` → `THE RICH ARE LEAVING.` → `ONE CARRIAGE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the privilege. Charles was made a cardinal very young, because his uncle was the pope: exactly the kind of favoritism reformers complained about. Instead of enjoying it, he worked hard in Rome to help bring the Council of Trent to its close. Second, the reform. The council told bishops to live in their own dioceses and care for their people. That sounds obvious, but it answered a real problem: bishops who lived far away and simply drew the income. Charles moved to Milan and stayed. He visited parishes, opened seminaries to train priests, and pared down his own household. Not everyone loved him for it. Some resisted his reforms, and one group even tried to have him killed. Third, the plague. When the sickness came, he stayed and served. Tradition says he gave away his own goods, even his household hangings, to clothe the poor, and led processions of prayer through the city barefoot. Fourth, the shepherd. Some readers see in him Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." In the same chapter Jesus describes the hired hand who sees the wolf coming and runs. The difference, the chapter suggests, isn't courage. It's whose sheep they are. Charles treated Milan as his own. The rich young cardinal is remembered for something simple. He stayed.
screen: `A CARDINAL BY FAVORITISM.` · `REFORM: LIVE WITH YOUR PEOPLE.` · `THE PLAGUE, AND THE BARE FEET.` · `THE SHEPHERD AND THE HIRED HAND.` · then, large: `THE GOOD SHEPHERD GIVETH HIS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of a place, a person or a task you'd like to escape right now, and just notice the pull to leave, without deciding anything big. Then ask whether there's one small way to stay a little longer, with care. If you pray, ask for the strength to stay; if you don't, just breathe, and stay with the question.

854.title: Peter Canisius (1521–1597)
854.hook: he wrote simple catechisms for the people of Germany
854.howItsDone: Catholic parishes run catechism classes for children and adults preparing for the sacraments, and the Church publishes catechisms, from short ones for families to the full Catechism of the Catholic Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles Borromeo came back into a city with plague. Your line was he stayed. This week went from a cave at Manresa to the Jesuits, Xavier, Teresa's cart, Philip's laughter and Milan. Today, a man with a pen.

What is a Christian? A child should be able to answer that. So should a farmer, a baker, a soldier. But in German lands, in a century of fierce argument about faith, the shouting could drown out the explaining. A Jesuit from the Netherlands, Peter Canisius, decided to try something modest. Short questions. Short answers. A little book a family could keep by the fire, and a child could learn by heart.
screen: `WHAT IS A CHRISTIAN?` → `MORE SHOUTING THAN EXPLAINING.` → `A LITTLE BOOK BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A catechism teaches by question and answer. Someone asks, someone answers, and the answer is short enough to remember. It's how a parent teaches a child, and it's very old. Canisius didn't invent it; he made it work for his age. Then, the sizes. He wrote a longer catechism for students and teachers, and a small one for children and ordinary people. Same faith, different doorways: a farmer and a professor need different books. Then, the tone. This was the age of the Reformation, of bitter pamphlets on both sides. In his letters, Canisius urged fellow Catholics toward patience and charity with those who disagreed, and warned that harshness drove people further away. His catechisms set out what the Church teaches, plainly, more than they attack anyone. Last, the root. Some readers connect teaching the faith with a line in the First Letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." A reason, not a lecture. Canisius traveled constantly, preached, founded schools, and wrote. His small books were printed again and again, and the Church later named him a Doctor of the Church. But his real gift was simple: he trusted that a hard truth could be said in simple words.
screen: `QUESTION AND ANSWER.` · `A BIG BOOK AND A SMALL ONE.` · `PATIENCE, NOT HARSHNESS.` · `A REASON FOR THE HOPE.` · then, large: `SIMPLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Imagine a child, or a curious friend, asking you one honest question: what do you believe, or hold most deeply, and why? Try to answer in two or three plain sentences, the way Canisius would have written it; if you're still searching, say that simply too, since that's an honest answer. If you pray, ask for the right words.
Catechism. A book that teaches the faith by short questions and answers, like the ones Peter Canisius wrote for scholars and for children.
